newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Italy on "right track" for EMU, says EU presidency.
newsitem.headline: Italy on "right track" for EMU, says EU presidency.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker of Luxembourg, which holds the European Union presidency, said on Monday that Italy was on the "right track" to take part in a single European currency due for launch on January 1, 1999.
Juncker said a working visit on Monday by Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi had been "very instructive", with monetary union and EU enlargement among topics discussed.

"The EU presidency thinks Italy can show an altogether remarkable performance concerning its preparations for entry into economic and monetary union," Juncker said at a joint news conference with Prodi.
They were accompanied by Italy's Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini and Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco.
Juncker, whose country took over the rotating EU presidency on July 1, highlighted what he called Italy's "astonishing performance" in controlling its inflation.

A decision on those taking part in the single currency will be taken next year, based on 1997 finances, and Italy's chances of joining have been bolstered by increased debate over whether the Maastricht Treaty entry criteria might be interpreted less strictly than previously thought.

Prodi, who has pledged to cut the Italian budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product as needed, said Italy was also making a big effort to increase its rate of economic growth and would maintain its fight against inflation.
It was also making efforts to reduce its high debt.
"As a consequence of the planned action there will be a small decrease in the debt to GDP ratio for the next year...and we think this trend will go on in the future," he said.

On the EU's planned enlargement into central and eastern Europe, Juncker said Italy and Luxembourg agreed that there was no question of giving the impression to applicant countries that they would never have the right to join the 15-nation bloc.
"We think all the countries that have shown their intention to join the European Union have a vocation to become members," Juncker said.

The European Commission last week recommended enlargement talks begin with five former communist countries plus Cyprus, leaving out another five disappointed applicants. An EU summit in Luxembourg December will decide on the proposal.
Juncker said Monday's meetings had also discussed future financing of the EU in the context of enlargement.
"The December summit ought to agree on the broad lines of financing and the architecture of structural policy for the years ahead," he said, though a full agreement was unlikely.
He added there was a "need for clarification so that everyone knows in which direction the debate on future financing of the Eureopan Union could evolve".
